Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist widely considered one of the two pillars of modern physics, standing alongside quantum mechanics. He developed the special and general theories of relativity, which revolutionized our concepts of space, time, mass, and gravity. He also made foundational contributions to quantum theory and statistical mechanics, earning the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the law of the photoelectric effect.

In 1905, Einstein formulated special relativity, postulating that the laws of physics are identical for all non-accelerating observers and that the speed of light in a vacuum is constant regardless of the observer's motion. From this came the most famous equation in science: E equals mc squared. Energy and mass are equivalent; they are the same thing at different scales.

A decade later, in 1915, he developed the theory of general relativity, describing gravity not as an attractive force pulling objects together, but as the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime caused by the presence of mass and energy. This was a complete reimagining of gravity itself. He predicted the existence of gravitational waves and gravitational lensing — the bending of light by gravity. In 1919, Arthur Eddington confirmed this prediction during a solar eclipse, making Einstein an international celebrity overnight.

That same year of 1905 — his miraculous year — Einstein also explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that light consists of discrete wave-packets of energy called photons, a discovery that became foundational for wave-particle duality. He mathematically explained Brownian motion, providing the first definitive proof that atoms and molecules actually exist. He later co-developed Bose-Einstein statistics and predicted the Bose-Einstein condensate, a state of matter occurring near absolute zero.

In 1935, Einstein co-authored the famous EPR paradox paper with Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen to challenge the completeness of quantum mechanics. He argued against what he called "spooky action at a distance" — what we now call quantum entanglement. He spent his later years at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study trying to formulate a Unified Field Theory, and he famously rejected the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics, stating that God does not play dice with the universe.

In 1939, Einstein wrote a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt warning of German nuclear weapons research. This letter catalyzed the creation of the Manhattan Project. Max Planck's quantum constant became the key to Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect. Niels Bohr was his chief intellectual rival, and they engaged in famous debates at the Solvay Conferences over the interpretation of quantum mechanics. Einstein endorsed Louis de Broglie's hypothesis that matter waves exist, helping it gain widespread acceptance. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle became one of Einstein's prime targets for philosophical criticism, through various thought experiments.
